review.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al.)
review.publisher: OpenAI and Johns Hopkins University (arXiv preprint, cs.LG)
review.as_of: 2020-01-23 (v1). Follow-ups checked: Chinchilla arXiv 2203.15556 v1 2022-03-29; Dettmers and Zettlemoyer arXiv 2212.09720 v2 2023-02-28; Kumar et al. arXiv 2411.04330 2024-11-07 (abstract only)
review.access_notes: I downloaded the PDFs of 2001.08361, 2203.15556 and 2212.09720 with curl, and the export.arxiv.org abstract pages for those three plus 2411.04330, into $SCRATCH/src/arxiv-scaling-laws/. I converted the PDFs with pdftotext -layout and quoted every number below from that raw text. I did not use WebFetch. For 2411.04330 I read only the abstract, not the full paper.
review.credibility_reason: This is a primary, heavily cited empirical paper from the lab that trained GPT-2 and GPT-3. The numbers come from its own training runs. Its limits are age (2020), scale (models with 768 to 1.5B non-embedding parameters, WebText2 only, 1024-token context) and its metric (pretraining cross-entropy loss, not task quality). Chinchilla later revised its compute-optimal allocation, and Chinchilla's authors explain why: Kaplan used a fixed learning-rate schedule and token count for all runs. The paper is credible for what it measured and not directly usable for choosing a quantized, instruction-tuned, MoE coding model in 2026.
review.summary: Kaplan et al. show that pretraining loss falls as a smooth power law in non-embedding parameters N, data D and compute C, and that model shape matters little. Larger models are more sample-efficient. In their compute-optimal recipe, model size grows faster than data (N proportional to C^0.73). For local model choice, the useful and still valid point is qualitative: at a fixed training recipe and data, more parameters means lower loss, with diminishing returns (doubling N multiplies loss by about 0.95). The paper says nothing about quantization, MoE, instruction tuning or RLHF, long context, coding or agentic tasks, or inference-time memory budgets. Its one inference remark (Appendix B) is that using a smaller model is useful once inference cost is counted. Chinchilla (2022) overturned the allocation: parameters and tokens should scale about equally, roughly 20 tokens per parameter (1B to 20.2B tokens, 10B to 205.1B tokens). Modern small models are trained far beyond that, which is why a 2026 27B to 35B model beats much larger 2020-era models. Dettmers and Zettlemoyer (2022/2023) is the paper that actually answers "bigger model at lower bits or smaller model at higher bits". At a fixed total memory, 4-bit with small blocks was almost always the best trade on zero-shot accuracy across OPT, BLOOM, Pythia and GPT-2 (19M to 176B). Zero-shot 3-bit usually lost, but one-shot methods (GPTQ with blocking) improved low-bit results. Kumar et al. (2024) add that post-training quantization hurts more as models are trained on more data, a caution for today's heavily overtrained small models. In practice for this 16 GB laptop: prefer the largest model that fits at about 4 bits (Q4_K_M, IQ4_XS, AWQ or GPTQ-4bit, NVFP4/MXFP4) with room left for the KV cache. Treat 3-bit only as a measured exception, never a default. Do not go above 4 to 5 bits if that forces a smaller model, unless the larger model cannot fit at 4 bits.

findings.claim: L(N) = (Nc/N)^alphaN with alphaN ~ 0.076 and Nc ~ 8.8e13 non-embedding parameters, for models trained to convergence on large datasets. Doubling parameters multiplies loss by 2^-alphaN = 0.95.

L(D): alphaD ~ 0.095, Dc ~ 5.4e13 tokens. L(Cmin): alphaC ~ 0.050, Cc ~ 3.1e8 PF-days. The constants depend on vocabulary and tokenization and 'do not have a fundamental meaning', so they cannot be compared across tokenizers.
Within reasonable limits, performance depends very weakly on depth vs width and attention heads. Scale (N, D, C) dominates.

'Large models are more sample-efficient than small models, reaching the same level of performance with fewer optimization steps and using fewer data points.' This is a training-time property. It says nothing direct about inference quality per GB.
N proportional to Cmin^0.73, B to Cmin^0.24, S to Cmin^0.03, and D proportional to N^0.74. Per Chinchilla's reading, a 10x compute increase should go to a 5.5x larger model and only 1.8x more tokens.
The penalty depends on N^0.74/D: each 8x increase in model size needs only about 5x more data to avoid it.

Appendix B: models between 0.6x and 2.2x the compute-optimal size cost only about 20% more training compute, and 'Using a smaller model is useful when accounting for the cost inference.' This is the paper's only inference-side guidance.

Models from 768 to 1.5B non-embedding parameters, 22M to 23B tokens of WebText2, context 1024 for most runs, decoder-only dense Transformers plus LSTM comparisons. The metric is cross-entropy loss, not downstream accuracy.

Raw-text search of the paper: 0 occurrences of 'quantiz', 'precision', 'instruct', 'downstream' and 'mixture'. The 2 'sparse' hits are reference titles (sparse transformers, block-sparse GPU kernels). The paper does not cover quantization, MoE, instruction or RL tuning, long context, coding or agentic tasks, or inference memory and latency.

Parameters and tokens should scale in equal proportions. Optimal-N exponent a = 0.50 / 0.49 / 0.46 across three approaches, vs Kaplan 0.73. Chinchilla, at 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens with Gopher's compute, outperforms Gopher 280B, GPT-3 175B and MT-NLG 530B.
Compute-optimal token counts: 400M parameters to 8.0B tokens, 1B to 20.2B, 10B to 205.1B, 67B to 1.5T. That is about 20 tokens per parameter, which applies to training compute, not inference.

Kaplan used a fixed number of training tokens and a fixed learning-rate schedule for all models, and most runs were under 100M parameters. Matching the cosine schedule to the token count changes the conclusion.

Chinchilla 'uses substantially less compute for fine-tuning and inference': at fixed quality, a smaller, better-trained model is cheaper to serve. This is the basis for today's small models trained far beyond 20 tokens per parameter.

With more than 35,000 zero-shot experiments on OPT, BLOOM, BLOOMZ, Pythia/NeoX and GPT-2 (19M to 176B), at a fixed total of model bits, lowering precision from 16 to 4 bits raises zero-shot accuracy. At 3 bits the trend reverses. '4-bit precision is almost universally optimal for total model bits and zero-shot accuracy.' The only exception is BLOOM-176B, where 3-bit was 'slightly but not significantly better'.

Use 4-bit by default, a block size of 128 or lower, and a float or quantile data type. 'If trade-offs in total model bits or predictive performance are desired, keep the precision in 4-bit but vary the number of parameters of the model instead.'

Higher precision makes sense when memory can hold a higher-bit version of a model but not a larger model at 4 bits. Their example: a 48 GB GPU fits 66B at 5-bit but not 175B at 4-bit, so 66B at 5-bit is preferable.

GPTQ with blocking beats zero-shot 3-bit Float on WikiText-2 perplexity, at block sizes 1024 / 256 / 64: 2-bit GPTQ 11.84 / 10.00 / 9.18 vs 3-bit Float 13.26 / 10.38 / 9.99. 3-bit GPTQ without blocking scales poorly. One-shot methods are 'very promising for low-bit precisions'.

At small batch sizes, inference latency is set by loading weights from memory. Caching is ineffective below batch sizes of about 60 (RTX 3090) or 200 (RTX 4090). Total model bits therefore track decode latency. The paper adds that these laws stop holding at large, busy-server batch sizes.

Only zero-shot accuracy (LAMBADA and similar) and perplexity on 2022 base models. No coding, tool-use or agentic evaluation, no MoE, and no modern instruction or RL-tuned models (BLOOMZ is the only tuned family). Only round-to-nearest-style zero-shot methods are covered systematically. GPTQ, learned codebooks, and later k-quant/imatrix, AWQ and QAT methods are not.

'The degradation introduced by post-training quantization increases as models are trained on more data, eventually making additional pretraining data actively harmful.' Fit on 465 pretraining runs, validated up to 1.7B parameters on 26B tokens. Implication: modern small models trained on many trillions of tokens may lose more at low bits than 2022 OPT or BLOOM did.

For a fixed VRAM budget, prefer more parameters at about 4 bits (with small blocks or a calibrated method) over fewer parameters at 8 or 16 bits. Avoid 3-bit or lower unless a calibrated method (imatrix k-quants, GPTQ or AWQ with groups, QAT) and a task eval on this machine show it beats the 4-bit alternative. This is an inference drawn from 2212.09720 and 2411.04330. No paper here tested coding agents, MoE or 2026 models.

conflicts.baseline_claim: Pick 2: Qwen3.8-27B with llama.cpp unsloth UD-Q3_K_XL, all on GPU, 12.24 GiB.
conflicts.source_claim: Dettmers and Zettlemoyer (2212.09720): with zero-shot quantization, 3-bit loses to 4-bit at equal total bits in almost all families tested. One-shot or blocked methods narrow the gap, and the paper calls them promising.
conflicts.assessment: This is a soft tension, not a contradiction. UD-Q3_K_XL is a mixed-precision, imatrix-calibrated, block-quantized format, closer to the 'one-shot plus blocking' case the paper calls promising than to the zero-shot 3-bit it found worse. Kumar et al. (2411.04330) also suggest heavily trained modern models lose more under post-training quantization. So the KB should label Qwen3.8-27B at about 3.5 bits as needing a measured comparison against a 4-bit alternative of similar size (for example the Gemma 4 26B-A4B QAT Q4_0 at 13.45 GiB, or a Q4 dense model that fits) on the user's coding tasks. It should not be an unconditional pick.

conflicts.baseline_claim: Several picks are MoE models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, Nemotron 3.5 30B-A3B, Qwen3-Coder-Next) chosen partly because of their total parameter count.
conflicts.source_claim: Kaplan's laws use dense non-embedding parameter count, and neither Kaplan nor Dettmers studies MoE. Chinchilla mentions MoE scaling only in related work (Clark et al. 2022), noting diminishing returns as experts increase.
conflicts.assessment: Not a conflict, but a scope warning. None of these papers supports comparing MoE total or active parameters against dense parameters on one scale. The KB should not cite Kaplan or Dettmers to justify a MoE pick.

agreements: The baseline's default of about 4-bit weights (Q4_K_M, Q4_0 QAT, IQ4_XS, MXFP4/NVFP4) for the largest model that fits matches Dettmers and Zettlemoyer's recommendation: use 4-bit by default and vary parameter count rather than precision (arXiv 2212.09720, sections 1 and 7).
The baseline's view that decode speed on this laptop is bound by memory bandwidth (896 GB/s) matches 2212.09720 section 2.1: at small batch sizes, latency is set by the bytes of weights loaded.

The baseline treats estimates from config.json and file sizes as estimates. None of these papers offers numbers for any 2026 model or for RTX 5080 hardware, so nothing here can be used as a measurement for this machine.

kb_notes.note: Rule of thumb for a fixed VRAM budget: choose the largest model that fits at about 4 bits with room for the KV cache, rather than a smaller model at 8 or 16 bits. Dettmers and Zettlemoyer found 4-bit 'almost universally optimal for total model bits and zero-shot accuracy' across 19M to 176B models, and recommend 'keep the precision in 4-bit but vary the number of parameters' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720).

Go above 4 bits only when the next larger model cannot fit at 4 bits. The paper's own example: a 48 GB GPU fits 66B at 5-bit but not 175B at 4-bit, so 66B at 5-bit is preferable (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720, section 7).

Treat 3-bit and lower as an exception that needs a local A/B test. In 2212.09720, zero-shot 3-bit lost to 4-bit at equal bits, while calibrated, blocked methods (GPTQ with block size 64: 2-bit WikiText-2 perplexity 9.18 vs 9.99 for zero-shot 3-bit Float) narrowed the gap. Kumar et al. report that post-training quantization hurts more as models are trained on more data (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04330), which applies to today's heavily overtrained small models.

Kaplan et al. 2020 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) show that pretraining loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute: doubling non-embedding parameters multiplies loss by about 0.95. The fits come from dense models of at most 1.5B parameters on WebText2. The paper does not cover quantization, MoE, instruction tuning, coding or agentic tasks, so it gives no direct guidance on which quantized 2026 model to run.

Parameter count alone does not rank models across generations. Chinchilla (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) showed that a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beats 175B to 530B models trained on fewer tokens, with about 20 tokens per parameter as the compute-optimal point. Modern open models are trained far beyond that, so compare current evals (benchmarks, our own tests), not sizes across model families or years.

No paper reviewed here (2001.08361, 2203.15556, 2212.09720) studies MoE models, so total or active parameter counts of MoE models (for example 35B-A3B) cannot be placed on the same scaling curve as dense models. Choose MoE models from task evals and measured speed on this laptop.

Quantization choice: use block-quantized 4-bit formats (Q4_K_M, IQ4_XS, Q4_0 QAT) as the default. Dettmers and Zettlemoyer recommend a block size of 128 or lower and found block size and data type to be the main levers for low-bit quality (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720). Keep a 3-bit build such as UD-Q3_K_XL only after it beats a 4-bit alternative of similar size on our own coding tasks.

arXiv 2001.08361 (Kaplan et al., OpenAI, 2020-01-23): paper, high credibility for pretraining loss scaling in dense models up to 1.5B parameters, superseded on compute-optimal allocation by arXiv 2203.15556 (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind, 2022-03-29). Not a source for quantization or model picks. For bits vs parameters, cite arXiv 2212.09720 (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, v2 2023-02-28) and arXiv 2411.04330 (Kumar et al., 2024-11-07).

Why bits per weight predict local decode speed: at batch size 1 the GPU spends its time loading weights, not computing (caching is ineffective below batch about 60 on an RTX 3090 or 200 on an RTX 4090), so latency tracks total model bits (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720, section 2.1). This holds for single-user OpenCode use, not for large-batch serving.

gaps: None of the papers evaluates coding, tool calling or agentic tasks, or long context, so the 'bits vs parameters' advice is extrapolated from zero-shot accuracy and perplexity.
No study of MoE models under quantization, and none of modern formats in use here: llama.cpp k-quants with imatrix, unsloth dynamic UD quants, AWQ, NVFP4/MXFP4, QAT Q4_0.
I read only the abstract of 2411.04330 (Scaling Laws for Precision). Its validation scale (up to 1.7B parameters, 26B tokens) is far below the 27B to 35B models in the baseline.
There is no KV-cache quantization guidance in any of these papers. KV q8_0 decisions need other sources.
A local A/B on the user's coding tasks would settle it: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q3_K_XL against a 4-bit alternative of similar size.
review.methodology: I read the baseline file (current-knowledge.md). I downloaded the arXiv PDFs and abstract pages with curl into the scratchpad src/arxiv-scaling-laws directory, converted the PDFs with pdftotext -layout, and grepped and read the summary, equation, caveat, table and limitations sections. Every number is quoted from that raw text. Python ran only with -I to parse one abstract page. Nothing was installed and nothing was written to the project directory.

verdicts.item: Publisher, type, as-of: Kaplan et al., OpenAI plus Johns Hopkins (Kaplan), arXiv preprint, v1 2020-01-23; follow-up dates
verdicts.evidence: arXiv API (export.arxiv.org/api/query): 2001.08361 published/updated 2020-01-23T03:59:20Z; 2203.15556 2022-03-29; 2212.09720 published 2022-12-19, updated 2023-02-28; 2411.04330 published 2024-11-07. PDF header: 'Johns Hopkins University, OpenAI' for Kaplan, all other authors OpenAI.
verdicts.correction: Minor: 2411.04330 also has a later version updated 2024-11-30; cite published 2024-11-07, latest version 2024-11-30.

verdicts.item: Eq 1.1-1.3 constants: alphaN ~0.076, Nc ~8.8e13; alphaD ~0.095, Dc ~5.4e13 tokens; alphaC ~0.050, Cc ~3.1e8 PF-days; 2^-alphaN = 0.95
verdicts.evidence: 2001.08361.txt lines 216, 219, 224, 264: 'αN ∼ 0.076, Nc ∼ 8.8 × 10^13 (non-embedding parameters)', 'αD ∼ 0.095, Dc ∼ 5.4 × 10^13 (tokens)', '∼ 0.050, Cmin_c ∼ 3.1 × 10^8 (PF-days)', 'smaller by a factor 2^−αN = 0.95'. Measured fits on the authors' own training runs.

verdicts.item: Experimental scope: 768 to 1.5B non-embedding params, 22M to 23B tokens, context 1024 for most runs
verdicts.evidence: 2001.08361 section 3 (txt lines 407-411): 'ranging in size from 768 to 1.5 billion non-embedding parameters', 'ranging from 22 million to 23 billion tokens', 'Context length (1024 for most runs...)'.

verdicts.item: Kaplan allocation N ~ Cmin^0.73, B ~ Cmin^0.24, S ~ Cmin^0.03, D ~ N^0.74; 8x model needs ~5x data; Chinchilla reading 5.5x model / 1.8x tokens per 10x compute
verdicts.evidence: 2001.08361 eq 6.1/6.2 and table lines 1224-1229 (pN=0.73, pB=0.24, pS=0.03); line 125-126 'increase the model size 8x, we only need to increase the data by roughly 5x'; 2203.15556 lines 48-49 'size of the model should increase 5.5× while the number of training tokens should only increase 1.8×'.

verdicts.item: Appendix B inference remark: 0.6x to 2.2x optimal size at ~20% more compute; 'Using a smaller model is useful when accounting for the cost inference'
verdicts.evidence: 2001.08361 txt lines 1352-1353 verbatim (including the paper's typo 'the cost inference'). Labeled 'computed' correctly: derived from eq B.16, not a separate measurement.

verdicts.item: 'Not covered' grep: 0 hits for quantiz, precision, instruct, downstream, mixture; 2 'sparse' hits are reference titles
verdicts.evidence: My grep -ci on fresh pdftotext output: quantiz 0, precision 0, instruct 0, downstream 0, mixture 0, sparse 2 (lines 1743 'sparse transformers' and 1763 'block-sparse weights', both references).

verdicts.item: Chinchilla: a = 0.50/0.49/0.46; Table 3 tokens 400M->8.0B, 1B->20.2B, 10B->205.1B, 67B->1.5T; Kaplan used fixed tokens and LR schedule, many runs <100M
verdicts.evidence: 2203.15556 Table 2 lines 424-426; Table 3 lines 435-438 (titled 'Estimated optimal training FLOPs and training tokens', so 'computed' label is right); lines 147 and 158-159 'fixed number of training tokens and learning rate schedule', 'many being less than 100M parameters'.

verdicts.item: Chinchilla on MoE: 'diminishing returns as experts increase' (Clark et al. 2022)
verdicts.evidence: 2203.15556 lines 160-163: Clark et al. show 'the scaling with number of experts diminishes as the model size increases'.
verdicts.correction: Restate as: the benefit from adding experts shrinks as model size grows (per Clark et al., cited in Chinchilla related work). Does not change the scope-warning conclusion.

verdicts.item: Dettmers and Zettlemoyer: >35,000 zero-shot experiments, 19M-176B, '4-bit precision is almost universally optimal', BLOOM-176B 3-bit 'slightly but not significantly better'; recommendations (4-bit default, block size 128 or lower, float/quantile type, 'keep the precision in 4-bit but vary the number of parameters'); 48 GB GPU 66B 5-bit example
Table 1 WikiText-2 perplexity, block 1024/256/64: 2-bit GPTQ 11.84/10.00/9.18 vs 3-bit Float 13.26/10.38/9.99; caching ineffective below batch ~60 (RTX 3090) / 200 (RTX 4090)
verdicts.evidence: 2212.09720.txt lines 460-464 (Table 1) and lines 110-112 'below 60 or 200 for an RTX 3090 or RTX 4090 GPU. As such, caching is ineffective below these batch sizes'. Note: Table 1 does not name the model in its caption; the KB note should say 'WikiText-2 perplexity, model as in the paper's Table 1' rather than imply a specific model.

verdicts.item: Kumar et al. 2411.04330 abstract: PTQ degradation grows with more training data; 465 runs, validated up to 1.7B params / 26B tokens
verdicts.evidence: arXiv API summary: 'the degradation introduced by post-training quantization increases as models are trained on more data, eventually making additional pretraining data actively harmful' and 'We fit on over 465 pretraining runs and validate our predictions on model sizes up to 1.7B parameters trained on up to 26B tokens.'

verdicts.item: Conflict 1: baseline pick 2 Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q3_K_XL 12.24 GiB vs 3-bit findings; soft tension, needs local A/B vs 4-bit (e.g. Gemma 4 26B-A4B QAT Q4_0 13.45 GiB)
verdicts.evidence: current-knowledge.md lines 68-69 match the quoted baseline sizes. Assessment is fair: the paper's negative 3-bit result is for zero-shot round-to-nearest; calibrated/blocked methods are called promising, so 'needs measurement' rather than 'contradiction' is correct.

verdicts.item: Conflict 2: MoE picks not supported by dense scaling papers (scope warning, not conflict)
verdicts.evidence: Kaplan grep shows no MoE content; Dettmers families (OPT, BLOOM, BLOOMZ, Pythia, GPT-2) are all dense; Chinchilla mentions MoE only in related work (lines 160-166).

check.credibility_note: High is right for what the papers measured: these are primary empirical papers with their own training/eval runs, and the review correctly limits them to dense pretraining-loss scaling (Kaplan, Chinchilla) and zero-shot quantization trade-offs on 2022 base models (Dettmers). It also correctly says none of them is a measurement for 2026 models, MoE, coding agents or RTX 5080 hardware. No laptop or desktop RTX 5080 numbers appear in any of them, so there is no hardware mix-up to flag.
check.summary: The review holds up after I re-opened the sources myself. I fetched all three PDFs again into a fresh directory, $SCRATCH/src/arxiv-check2/, converted them with pdftotext -layout, and pulled metadata and the 2411.04330 abstract from the export.arxiv.org API. Every load-bearing number I checked matches the raw text exactly: the Kaplan constants and exponents, the 0.95 factor, the experiment scope, the Appendix B inference remark, the Chinchilla exponents and Table 3 token counts, the Dettmers 4-bit claims and recommendations, Table 1 perplexities, the RTX 3090/4090 batch thresholds, and the 465-run / 1.7B / 26B scope of Kumar et al. The measured vs computed labels are correct, including Chinchilla Table 3, which the paper itself calls estimated projections. Both baseline conflicts are real and fairly framed, and the baseline values they cite (12.24 GiB for UD-Q3_K_XL, 13.45 GiB for Gemma QAT Q4_0) match current-knowledge.md lines 68-69. Two corrections, both minor. First, Chinchilla's note on Clark et al. says the gain from more experts shrinks as model size grows, not "diminishing returns as experts increase". Second, 2411.04330 was last updated 2024-11-30, a later version than the 2024-11-07 first release the review cites. One wording caveat: the Table 1 caption does not name the model, so the KB note should not tie those perplexities to a specific model.
